form.current-chamber: IN THE SENATE OF THE UNITED STATES

action.action-desc: Mr. Cassidy introduced the following bill; which was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions

form.official-title: To require the Office for Civil Rights of the Department of Health and Human Services to conduct a study and issue a report on the de-identification of data pursuant to privacy regulations.

section.text: This Act may be cited as the Health Data De-identification Report Act.

section.header: Study and report by the HHS Office for Civil Rights

subsection.text: The Office for Civil Rights of the Department of Health and Human Services, in cooperation with the National Institute of Standards and Technology, shall conduct a study that considers and compares the effectiveness and validity of safe harbor and expert determination as methods of carrying out the de-identification of data required under section 164.514 of title 45, Code of Federal Regulations (as in effect on the date of enactment of this Act), and shall submit to Congress a report on such study not later than 270 days of the date of enactment of this Act.
The study and report under subsection (a) shall consider—

paragraph.text: any known instances where data that was de-identified as required under section 164.514 of title 45, Code of Federal Regulations (as in effect on the date of enactment of this Act) became re-identified, even partially, and, with respect to each such instance, how such re-identification occurred and any harm incurred by any individual whose data was re-identified;

the frequency by which each of the safe harbor method and the expert determination method is used for the de-identification of data as described in subsection (a), and the sizes of the data sets on which each such method is used;
the costs of each such method of de-identification, and the relative utility of the data that is de-identified through each such method;
which of the 2 methods of de-identification renders data less likely to be easily re-identifiable;
whether either such method removes information that would help address health care disparities, thereby making it more difficult to address such disparities;
which of the 2 methods is most commonly used for purposes of medical research, and the benefits and disadvantages of using each such method for such purpose;
the risk of re-identification by each of the 2 methods, especially when the resulting de-identified dataset will be accessible by entities that have access to additional data;
whether or not there are use cases that cannot be performed using data de-identified by either of the 2 methods; and
the ease or difficulty of expert determination, taking into consideration cost, accessibility, and qualifications of experts.
